description: Behavior cases for staff+ scope selection: level-relative leverage, under-owned problems, matching archetypes to strengths, screening the traps, and an explicit rationale + NOT-doing list.

cases.prompt: I'm a staff engineer and I'm not sure what to focus on next. Help me pick high-leverage scope.

assertions: Defines leverage relative to the staff level (multiplies others / sets direction), not more individual output.
Surfaces important UNDER-OWNED problems as the kind of candidate to look for (the gap between teams, the decision nobody is making), not just assigned work.

Because the prompt gives no strengths or org problems, asks one atomic discovery question for one of the missing facts before recommending (any candidate it sketches is matched to a leverage archetype and marked provisional), and states that the NOT-doing list follows the person's choice.
Names the traps the eventual scope must pass (only-fun, only-firefighting, too-narrow, invisible glue, over-reach).
Names visibility/attribution as a requirement for the eventual scope and hands past-impact documentation to promotion-packet-writer.

cases.prompt: I've spent the whole quarter firefighting incidents. I work constantly but feel like I'm not having staff-level impact.

assertions: Names firefighting as reactive senior execution, not staff-level leverage.
Redirects toward direction-setting or multiplier work (e.g. fixing the systemic cause of the fires so the team stops firefighting).
Recommends a scope with an explicit rationale (or asks the single discovery question) and states that the NOT-doing list, which protects focus, follows the person's choice.
Distinguishes working hard from having leverage.

cases.prompt: The most useful thing I could do is a bunch of cross-team coordination and integration glue, but nobody ever notices that work.

assertions: Recognizes glue work as often the highest real leverage AND the most invisible.
Keeps the scope but builds in visibility/attribution so it advances the engineer, not just the org.
Avoids the trap of high-value-but-uncredited work with no attribution path.
States how the impact will be made legible.

cases.prompt: The biggest problem is squarely in another staff engineer's owned area, but I want to just take it over since I'd do it better.

assertions: Flags taking over someone's owned scope as over-reach that creates conflict and undermines them.
Recommends aligning first (with the owner and management) rather than unilaterally claiming it (a Stop Condition).
Redirects toward genuine gaps or shared-area collaboration.
Does not endorse colonizing another's scope.

cases.prompt: We have 25 backlog items for the team — pick a prioritization framework and rank them.

assertions: Does not invoke staff-scope-selector: ranking a given team backlog is prioritization-frame-picker.
This skill selects an individual's high-leverage scope, not a team backlog ordering.

cases.prompt: I'm a senior engineer aiming for staff next cycle. I'm strongest at debugging build systems and writing clear design docs. Three candidate scopes: (1) own the flaky CI and slow test infrastructure that blocks about 40 engineers every week, which nobody owns today; (2) rewrite our billing service in Rust, which I'd enjoy but which works fine now; (3) define the cross-team API versioning strategy, which the platform team nominally owns but hasn't touched in a year. My manager hasn't said whether CI work would get any extra headcount. Don't pick for me: lay out the options, recommend one, and let me decide.

assertions: Treats the scope as the person's own choice rather than picking it for them, and defines leverage and non-scope in plain language.

For each of the three candidates gives why it fits (leverage type, fit with build-system debugging and design-doc strengths, org need), pros and cons, and time and attention, alignment setup, upkeep, and budget or headcount cost, marking the unknown CI headcount as unknown.

Screens the candidates against the traps: flags the Rust rewrite as only-fun, low-leverage scope and the API versioning strategy as the platform team's owned area that needs alignment first rather than being claimed unilaterally.
Recommends one candidate, explains why, names the fact that would change it, then asks exactly one atomic decision question, and says a NOT-doing list follows the person's choice.
